1.topic: Creation and the fall of humanity
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. tell the story of creation as written in Genesis 1 and 2;
2. explain how Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the garden (Genesis 3);
3. draw two moral lessons from the story.

## Materials

A Bible for each pair, a chart of the six days of creation, a picture of a garden.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: who made the sun, the river and the trees around our school? Take three answers and tell the pupils that today's story begins before anyone was born.

## Development

1. Read Genesis 1:1-31 slowly. List on the board what God made on each of the six days and what He said at the end of each day.
2. Read Genesis 1:26-28 and 2:15. Stress that humans were made in the image of God and were asked to care for the garden.
3. Read Genesis 2:16-17. Ask: what was the one rule God gave?
4. Read Genesis 3:1-24 in parts. Pause at verse 6 and ask pupils what the woman should have done.
5. Draw out the results: hiding, blaming, being sent out of Eden.

## Class activity

In groups of four, pupils act the conversation between the serpent and the woman, then say aloud the lesson they learnt.

## Evaluation

1. What was the last thing God made?
2. What did Adam say when God asked him about the fruit?

## Assignment

Write six sentences on what happened after Adam and Eve ate the fruit. Use Genesis 3:7-13.

reading.title: In the beginning
reading.content:
# In the beginning

The Bible begins with the book of **Genesis**, which means "beginning". It tells us that God made everything that exists.

## The six days

God made the world in an orderly way. On the first day He made light. On the second He made the sky. On the third He gathered the waters and made dry land and plants. On the fourth He made the sun, moon and stars. On the fifth He made fish and birds. On the sixth He made animals and, last of all, human beings. At the end of each day God saw that what He had made was good. On the seventh day God rested, and He blessed that day (Genesis 1 and 2:1-3).

## Humans in the image of God

Man and woman were different from all the other creatures. Genesis 1:27 says God made them in His own image. God told them to fill the earth and to look after the fish, the birds and every living thing. Adam was placed in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15). Work was good from the beginning.

## The one rule

God gave Adam one command. He could eat from every tree in the garden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. If he ate from it, he would die (Genesis 2:16-17).

## The fall

A serpent came to the woman and asked her whether God had really said they must not eat from any tree. Then it told her that she would not die, and that she would be like God. The woman saw that the fruit looked good, took it and ate it. She gave some to Adam, and he ate also (Genesis 3:1-6).

Straight away they felt shame. They sewed fig leaves together and hid when they heard God walking in the garden. When God asked what they had done, Adam blamed the woman, and the woman blamed the serpent (Genesis 3:7-13). God then spoke about the result of what they had done, and sent them out of the garden of Eden (Genesis 3:23-24).

## Lessons

- God's commands are for our good, so we should obey them.
- Temptation often begins with a doubt about what God has said.
- Excuses do not remove the blame. We must own up to our wrong.
- Sin brings consequences, but God still cared for Adam and Eve and clothed them (Genesis 3:21).

2.topic: Cain and Abel, Noah and the flood
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. tell the story of Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:1-16);
2. tell the story of Noah and the flood (Genesis 6:5-9:17);
3. state what each story teaches about obedience and justice.

## Materials

Bibles, a drawing of an ark, a chart with the headings "What happened" and "What it teaches".

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: have you ever been angry because someone else was praised? What did you feel like doing? Take two answers and link them to the first story.

## Development

1. Read Genesis 4:1-16. Establish that both brothers brought an offering, and that God was pleased with Abel's but not Cain's.
2. Discuss verses 6 and 7, where God speaks to Cain before the killing. Ask what Cain could have done.
3. Point out that God held Cain to account and that Abel's blood "cried out" for justice.
4. Read Genesis 6:5-22. List why God was grieved, why Noah was different and what Noah was told to build.
5. Read Genesis 7 and 8 in outline, then Genesis 9:8-17 for the rainbow promise.

## Class activity

In pairs, pupils fill the two-column chart for each story.

## Evaluation

1. Why was God not pleased with Cain's offering?
2. How long did Noah and his family stay in the ark?

## Assignment

Write four sentences on how you can show obedience to your parents at home, using Noah as your example.

reading.title: Two brothers, and a man who built a boat
reading.content:
# Two brothers, and a man who built a boat

## Cain and Abel

Adam and Eve had two sons. Cain became a farmer and Abel kept sheep. One day each brought an offering to God. Cain brought some of the crops from his farm. Abel brought the first and best of his flock. God was pleased with Abel and his offering, but He did not accept Cain's (Genesis 4:3-5).

Cain became very angry. God spoke to him and said that if he did what was right he would be accepted, and warned him that sin was waiting at his door like a wild animal. Cain did not listen. He took his brother into the field and killed him (Genesis 4:8).

God asked Cain where his brother was. Cain answered that he did not know, and asked, "Am I my brother's keeper?" God told him that Abel's blood was crying out from the ground. Cain was sent away from the land and had to wander (Genesis 4:9-16).

**What we learn:** anger that is not controlled can lead to terrible wrong; we should give God our best; God sees what is done in secret and punishes wrong; and we are responsible for the people around us.

## Noah and the flood

Many years later, the people on the earth had become so wicked that God was sorry He had made them. But Noah was a good man who walked with God. God told Noah to build a large boat, an **ark**, and gave him its size. Noah was to take his wife, his three sons, their wives, and a pair of every kind of animal (Genesis 6:9-22).

Noah did everything just as God commanded him. When the ark was ready, the rain fell for forty days and nights and the whole earth was covered with water. Only those in the ark were saved. After more than a year, the water went down, and Noah, his family and the animals came out onto dry ground (Genesis 7 and 8).

Noah built an altar and thanked God. God promised never again to destroy the earth with a flood, and gave the **rainbow** as a sign of His promise (Genesis 9:8-17).

**What we learn:**

- Noah obeyed God even when no rain had fallen and people may have laughed at him.
- God is just. He punishes wickedness, but He saves those who trust and obey Him.
- God keeps His promises.

3.topic: Abraham: the call, the covenant and Lot
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

1. describe God's call of Abram and the promises God made to him (Genesis 12:1-4);
2. explain the covenant between God and Abraham (Genesis 15 and 17);
3. describe how Abraham treated his nephew Lot (Genesis 13) and say what it teaches.

## Materials

Bibles, a map showing Ur, Haran and Canaan, a rope to use in the class activity.

## Starter (5 minutes)

Ask: what would you do if your parents told you the family was moving to a place they had not yet seen? How would you feel?

## Development

1. Locate Ur and Haran on the map. Read Genesis 12:1-4 and list God's commands and God's promises separately.
2. Explain that a covenant is a solemn agreement. Read Genesis 15:1-6 and 17:1-8. Note the new names Abraham and Sarah, and circumcision as the sign.
3. Read Genesis 13:1-13. Ask why the herdsmen quarrelled and what Abraham suggested.
4. Read Genesis 14:12-16 briefly to show that Abraham rescued Lot later.

## Class activity

Two pupils stand with a rope between them to show the land. Ask the class what Abraham did with the choice, and who chose first.

## Evaluation

1. What three promises did God make to Abram?
2. Why did Abraham let Lot choose first?

## Assignment

Write about a time when you let someone else have the first choice. How did it feel?

reading.title: The man who left home because God called
reading.content:
# The man who left home because God called

## The call

Abram lived in Haran with his wife Sarai, his father's family and his nephew Lot. God spoke to him and told him to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house and go to a land God would show him. God made promises: He would make Abram into a great nation, bless him, make his name great, and bless all the families of the earth through him (Genesis 12:1-3).

Abram was seventy-five years old. He did not ask where the land was. He took Sarai, Lot and all his belongings and set out for Canaan (Genesis 12:4-5). This is why Abraham is called a man of **faith**: he trusted God and obeyed Him without seeing the road.

## The covenant

A **covenant** is a serious agreement between two sides. Abram and Sarai had no child and were getting old. God told Abram in a vision to look up at the stars and count them, if he could, and said, "So shall your offspring be." Abram believed God (Genesis 15:1-6). Later God renewed the covenant. He changed Abram's name to **Abraham**, which means father of many nations, and Sarai's name to Sarah. God promised Abraham the land of Canaan for his descendants, and asked that every male in his household be circumcised as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:1-14).

## Abraham and Lot

Abraham and Lot both had large flocks and herds. The land could not hold them together and their herdsmen began to quarrel. Abraham went to Lot and said there must be no quarrel between them since they were relatives. He, the older man with the right to choose first, let Lot choose the land he wanted (Genesis 13:5-9).

Lot looked at the well-watered plain of the Jordan and chose it. It was beautiful, but it was near Sodom, whose people were wicked. Abraham stayed in Canaan. When enemy kings later carried Lot away, Abraham gathered his men, chased the kings and brought Lot home (Genesis 14:12-16).

## Lessons

- Trust and obey God even when we do not know where He is leading.
- God keeps His promises, even when they take a long time.
- Peace in the family is worth more than getting the best for ourselves.
- We should help our relatives in trouble.

reading.title: Two brothers, a coat, and a famine
reading.content:
# Two brothers, a coat, and a famine

## Isaac

Isaac was the son God had promised Abraham and Sarah. When he grew up, he married Rebekah, and God gave them twin sons, **Esau** and **Jacob**. Esau was born first and was a hunter. Jacob was quiet and stayed among the tents.

## Jacob and Esau

One day Esau came home from hunting, very hungry. Jacob had a pot of stew and would only give him some if he sold his **birthright**, the special place of the first-born son. Esau agreed and sold it for a meal (Genesis 25:29-34).

Later, when old Isaac was blind and wanted to bless Esau, Rebekah helped Jacob trick his father. Jacob covered his arms with goatskin so that he would feel hairy like Esau, and pretended to be his brother. Isaac blessed him (Genesis 27). Esau was furious, and Jacob had to flee to his uncle Laban's house in Haran.

## Joseph

Jacob had twelve sons. He loved Joseph most and gave him a coat of many colours. Joseph also told his brothers dreams in which they bowed down to him. The brothers hated him. One day, when Joseph came to them in the field, they sold him to traders who took him to Egypt (Genesis 37).

In Egypt, Joseph was a servant in Potiphar's house, was lied about and put in prison. God was with him there and he explained the dreams of two prisoners. Two years later, Pharaoh had troubling dreams and no one could explain them. Joseph said God was warning of seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and advised Pharaoh to store grain. Pharaoh made him the governor of Egypt, second only to himself (Genesis 41).

When the famine came, Joseph's brothers travelled to Egypt to buy food. Joseph recognised them and, after testing them, told them who he was. He did not take revenge. He said that God had sent him ahead to save many lives (Genesis 45:5-8). After their father died, he told them again not to be afraid. "You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good" (Genesis 50:20).

## Lessons

- Favouritism in a family causes jealousy.
- Deceit brings trouble even when it seems to win something.
- God can turn bad things around for good.
- Forgiveness is stronger than revenge.

reading.title: Moses, the law and the long walk
reading.content:
# Moses, the law and the long walk

## Moses is called

The Israelites had become slaves in Egypt. A cruel Pharaoh made them work hard and ordered their baby boys to be killed. Moses was saved as a baby, brought up in Pharaoh's palace, and ran away to Midian after he killed an Egyptian. There he became a shepherd.

One day, at Mount Horeb, Moses saw a bush that was burning but was not burnt up. God spoke from the bush and told him He had seen His people's suffering and had chosen Moses to bring them out of Egypt. Moses made excuses. He said he was nobody, that he could not speak well, and that Pharaoh would not listen. God promised to be with him and allowed his brother Aaron to speak for him (Exodus 3 and 4).

## Out of Egypt

Pharaoh refused to let the Israelites go until ten plagues had struck Egypt. After the last plague the Israelites left. Pharaoh's army chased them, and God opened a path through the Red Sea so that they crossed on dry ground (Exodus 14).

## The Ten Commandments

Three months later, at Mount Sinai, God gave Moses the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17). In short:

1. You shall have no other gods before Me.
2. You shall not make or bow down to idols.
3. You shall not misuse God's name.
4. Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
5. Honour your father and mother.
6. You shall not murder.
7. You shall not commit adultery.
8. You shall not steal.
9. You shall not give false evidence against your neighbour.
10. You shall not covet what belongs to another person.

The first four tell us how to treat God. The last six tell us how to treat other people.

## The journey

The Israelites were to go straight to Canaan, the Promised Land. At the edge of the land, twelve men were sent to spy it out. Ten of them brought back fearful reports, and the people refused to enter. For that lack of faith, they wandered in the wilderness for forty years (Numbers 13 and 14). Moses died on Mount Nebo, in sight of the land. His helper Joshua led the people across the Jordan.

## Lessons

- God hears the cry of those who suffer.
- God works through ordinary people who trust Him.
- God's laws protect us and keep society orderly.
- Fear and lack of faith can delay what God has promised.

reading.title: Leaders in hard times
reading.content:
# Leaders in hard times

After Joshua died, the Israelites settled in Canaan. They had no king. Again and again they forgot the Lord and worshipped the idols of the nations around them. Then God allowed enemies to defeat and oppress them. When the people cried out, God raised a leader to rescue them. These leaders were called **judges** (Judges 2:16-19).

A judge was a leader chosen by God. Judges led the army in battle, and settled disputes among the people. But each time a judge died, the people went back to their old ways. This happened many times.

## Deborah

Deborah was a prophetess and judge. She sat under a palm tree, and the Israelites came to her to settle their quarrels. When King Jabin of Canaan had oppressed Israel for twenty years, Deborah told Barak, the commander, that God had commanded him to go to battle. Barak would only go if Deborah went with him. God gave Israel the victory, and Deborah and Barak sang a song of praise (Judges 4 and 5).

## Gideon

When the Midianites raided Israel's crops, Gideon was threshing wheat in secret. An angel called him a mighty warrior. Gideon doubted and asked for signs. When thirty-two thousand men gathered, God said there were too many, and reduced them to three hundred. Gideon divided them into three groups. Each man held a trumpet, and a clay jar with a burning torch inside. At night, they blew the trumpets, broke the jars and shouted. The Midianites panicked and fled (Judges 6 and 7). Gideon refused to be made king and said the Lord would rule over Israel (Judges 8:22-23).

## Samson

Samson was set apart to God from birth as a Nazirite, and was given great strength. His long hair was the sign. He used his strength against the Philistines, but he was weak in his choices. He told his secret to Delilah, who cut his hair, and the Philistines blinded him and put him in prison. At the end, he prayed to God, pushed down the pillars of the Philistine temple and died with his enemies (Judges 13 to 16).

## Samuel

Samuel was the last of the judges. He was also a prophet who anointed Israel's first king, Saul (1 Samuel 7 to 10).

## Lessons

- God cares for His people and answers when they cry to Him.
- A good leader trusts God more than numbers or strength.
- Disobedience leads to suffering; obedience leads to peace.

reading.title: Two announcements and a baby in Bethlehem
reading.content:
# Two announcements and a baby in Bethlehem

## John the Baptist

A priest named Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth were both old. They loved God, but had no child. One day, while Zechariah was burning incense in the temple, the angel **Gabriel** appeared to him and said that Elizabeth would have a son, whose name would be John. John would prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. Zechariah doubted because they were so old, so Gabriel told him he would not be able to speak until the child was born (Luke 1:5-20). When the baby was born, Zechariah wrote, "His name is John", and his speech returned at once (Luke 1:57-64).

## The Annunciation

Six months later, Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, a town in Galilee, to a young woman named **Mary**, who was engaged to Joseph. He greeted her as one who was highly favoured by God. Mary was troubled. The angel told her not to be afraid. She would have a son and was to call Him **Jesus**. He would be great, would be called the Son of the Most High, and His kingdom would never end. Mary asked how this could happen as she was not married. Gabriel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her. Mary replied, "I am the Lord's servant. May your word to me be fulfilled" (Luke 1:26-38). This announcement is called the **Annunciation**.

Joseph, too, was told by an angel in a dream to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because He would save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:18-25).

## The birth of Jesus

The Roman emperor Caesar Augustus ordered a census, and everyone had to go to their own town to be registered. Joseph and Mary travelled from Nazareth to Bethlehem. There was no room in the guest room, and Mary gave birth to her son there and laid Him in a manger, a feeding trough for animals (Luke 2:1-7).

An angel appeared to shepherds who were watching their sheep on the hills at night. The angel told them that a Saviour, Christ the Lord, had been born. The shepherds went to Bethlehem and found the baby as the angel had said. They returned praising God (Luke 2:8-20).

## Why it matters

- It shows that Jesus is the Son of God and the promised Saviour.
- Mary is an example of humble obedience and trust.
- God cares for ordinary people: the shepherds were the first to hear.

reading.title: From the river to the wedding
reading.content:
# From the river to the wedding

## The baptism

When Jesus was about thirty years old, He came from Galilee to the River Jordan, where John was baptising people who had repented of their sins. John tried to stop Him, saying he himself needed to be baptised by Jesus. Jesus replied that it was right to do this to fulfil all righteousness, so John agreed. As Jesus came up out of the water, heaven was opened. The Spirit of God came down like a dove and rested on Him, and a voice from heaven said, "This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:13-17).

## The temptation

Then the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. Jesus fasted for forty days and forty nights and became hungry. The devil came three times (Matthew 4:1-11).

1. The devil said, "If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread." Jesus answered, "Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God."
2. The devil took Him to the top of the temple and said, "Throw yourself down, for the angels will save you." Jesus answered, "Do not put the Lord your God to the test."
3. The devil showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and said he would give them if Jesus would bow down and worship him. Jesus answered, "Worship the Lord your God, and serve him only."

Each time, Jesus answered with the word of God, and the devil left. Angels came and looked after Him. Jesus shows us how to face temptation: know God's word, trust God and refuse to take a short cut.

## The first miracle

Soon after, Jesus, His mother and His disciples were invited to a wedding at Cana in Galilee. The wine ran out, which was a serious embarrassment for the host. Mary told Jesus, and then told the servants to do whatever He told them. Jesus asked them to fill six large stone jars with water. Then He told them to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. The water had become wine, and it was better than the wine they had first served (John 2:1-11). John calls this a **sign**, and it showed Jesus' glory so that His disciples believed in Him.

## Lessons

- Jesus identified with sinners in baptism, and so shows His humility.
- The word of God is our weapon against temptation.
- Jesus cares about ordinary needs, even at a wedding.

reading.title: Blessed are those who listen
reading.content:
# Blessed are those who listen

When Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on a mountainside, sat down, and His disciples came to Him. Then He taught them. His teaching, in Matthew chapters 5 to 7, is called the **Sermon on the Mount**. It tells us what life in the **Kingdom of God** looks like: how people live when God is their King.

## The Beatitudes

The word "beatitude" means a blessing. Jesus began by saying who is truly blessed (Matthew 5:3-10):

- Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. (Those who know they need God.)
- Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
- Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
- Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.
- Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.
- Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
- Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
- Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

The world says happy people are rich, strong and famous. Jesus says happy people are humble, merciful and peaceful, and that God looks after them.

## Salt and light

Jesus told His followers, "You are the salt of the earth" and "You are the light of the world." Salt gives taste and keeps food from spoiling. A lamp is put on a stand to give light to everyone in the house. So Christians should let their good deeds be seen, so that people praise God (Matthew 5:13-16).

## Do not worry

Jesus said we should not worry about what we will eat or wear. God feeds the birds and clothes the flowers, and we are worth much more than they are. We should "seek first his kingdom and his righteousness", and God will give us what we need (Matthew 6:25-34).

## The two builders

Jesus ended the sermon with a story. A wise man built his house on rock. When rain fell, floods rose and winds blew, the house did not fall. A foolish man built his house on sand. When the storm came, it fell with a great crash. Jesus said that anyone who hears His words and does them is like the wise man. Anyone who hears and does not do them is like the foolish man (Matthew 7:24-27).

## Lessons

- Real happiness comes from living God's way.
- Our lives should show Christ like salt and light.
- It is not enough to hear God's word; we must obey it.
